description: Alpine duchy in the southeastern march of the Empire (976–1335) controlling the Drave valley routes between Italy and the Danube basin; repeatedly granted and revoked from various dynasties as an imperial instrument of control, it passed to the Habsburgs in 1335 consolidating their southeastern German territorial base.

temporal.notes: Stem duchy; Habsburg acquisition 1335; polity continues past 1500, end_year_within_scope used in UI.

geographic.notes: Centroid approximate; polygon pending schematic or OHM sourcing.

lifecycle_phases.description: Carinthia established as a separate march/duchy under Ottonian reorganization.
Duchy under successive dynasties; Meinhard consolidation.
Henry of Bohemia and Carinthia; contested succession.
Habsburg inheritance; Carinthia absorbed into Austrian complex.

rise_factors.description: Eastern Alps valleys provided natural barriers against Hungarian incursions in the 10th century.
Integration into Habsburg and Luxembourg imperial networks secured Carinthia against external threats.
The Meinhard dynasty maintained consistent rule through the 13th century.
Carinthia controlled key Alpine passes linking Italy with the Danube basin, generating transit revenues and giving the duchy strategic importance to both the Holy Roman Empire and Venetian commerce.
Established as a march against Magyar incursions, Carinthia received imperial support and colonization incentives that built up its military and agricultural base in the 10th century.

decline_factors.description: Henry of Carinthia died in 1335 without male heirs, ending the Meinhard-Görz dynasty.
Habsburgs inherited Carinthia through prior treaties, absorbing it into Austrian domains.
Imperial politics made Carinthia a pawn in Habsburg-Luxembourg-Wittelsbach rivalry.
Carinthia passed to the Habsburgs in 1335 through inheritance from the Gorizia dynasty, becoming an integral part of the Habsburg hereditary lands and losing its separate ducal identity.
The Black Death severely reduced Carinthia's population, disrupting the mining economy around Villach and leaving administrative structures understaffed through the late 14th century.
